concept.name: Overnight rate
concept.definition: The interest rate on loans or deposits with a maturity of one business day, typically traded between financial institutions to manage daily reserve or cash positions. Key U.S. overnight rates include the effective federal funds rate (unsecured) and SOFR (secured by Treasury collateral).
concept.intuition: It is the price of borrowing money until tomorrow — the shortest-maturity interest rate in the financial system and the anchor for all longer rates.
concept.mechanics: Institutions lend and borrow cash for one day in money markets; transaction-level data are aggregated into published benchmarks (the New York Fed computes EFFR and SOFR as volume-weighted medians of overnight transactions). Central banks steer overnight rates to implement policy.
concept.failure_modes: Overnight rates can spike under collateral or reserve scarcity (e.g. the September 2019 repo spike), breaking the link with the policy target; month- and quarter-end reporting effects also distort measured rates.
concept.misconceptions: There is no single 'overnight rate': secured (repo/SOFR) and unsecured (fed funds) overnight rates coexist and can diverge because they price different risks and counterparties.
concept.example: On a typical day, a bank lending reserves to another bank overnight earns the federal funds rate, while a money market fund lending cash against Treasury collateral earns a rate near SOFR.

citations.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR)
